senses: An inaccurate statement or statistic believed to be true because of broad repetition, especially if cited in the media.
An interesting item of trivia; a minor fact.
ety: From fact + -oid (“similar, but not the same”); coined by American writer Norman Mailer in 1973 in Marilyn: A Biography, defined as "facts which have no existence before appearing in a magazine or newspaper, creations which are not so much lies as a product to manipulate emotion in the Silent Majority".
examples: Such hedging is necessitated by the lack of in-depth knowledge of the contents, which also gives free rein to the scripting of unsubstantiated factoids concerning the book.
Don't parade in front of the audience spewing every factoid you know on your topic. Only share the right information for that exact moment with that specific audience.

senses: A purplish-red colour, the color of fuchsin, an aniline dye.
ety: From New Latin, after the genus Fuchsia, itself named after German botanist Leonhart Fuchs (1501–1566).
examples: She tilted a hand topped with long rectangular nails in furious fuchsia towards her cheeks and fluttered the fingers, fanning.

senses: A place or pit from which sand is excavated.
A children’s play area consisting of a large container filled with sand.
A small-scale illustrative model of the theater of war in the Middle East.
ety: From Middle English sandpitte, sandpette, sandpütte, from Old English sandpytt (“sandpit”), equivalent to sand + pit.
examples: Originally designed to illustrate Kuwait and the oil pipelines, the 'sandpit', based on maps and photographs to a scale of 1:1,000,000, was extended to include other countries.

senses: The rearing of silkworms for the production of silk.
ety: Possibly borrowed from French sériculture, a modification of French sériciculture (“sericulture”) (or directly from sériciculture), from Late Latin sēricum (“Chinese goods, especially silk”) + French culture (“crop; culture”). Sēricum is derived from Latin sēricus (“of or pertaining to the Seres or Chinese; (by extension) made of silk, silken”), from Sēres (“northern Chinese people”), from Ancient Greek Σῆρες (Sêres, “the Chinese people; the land of the Chinese, China”), plural of Σήρ (Sḗr, “(rare, usually in plural) Chinese person; silkworm”), possibly from Old Chinese 絲 (*slɯ, “silk”).
examples: Numerous experiments have been made with a view to improving sericulture in India.

senses: A rotorcraft propelled by four rotors.
ety: From quad- + copter.
examples: In April, as an Air Canada Jazz flight was landing at Trudeau Airport, a drone came so close the pilot was able to identify it as a quadcopter.

senses: An acoustic guitar with a metal resonator.
ety: From the trade name Dobro, used by the Gibson Guitar Corporation, from Dopyera or Dopjera, the name of the inventors + brothers, and also a pun on Slovak dobro (“good”).
examples: The longest and most incandescent track is “Twilight Kingdom,” which includes Stuart Duncan on fiddle, Jerry Douglas on dobro and David Grier on guitar.

senses: To sit with the limbs spread out.
To spread out in a disorderly fashion; to straggle.
ety: From Middle English spraulen, from Old English spreawlian (“move convulsively”), ultimately through a Proto-Germanic form cognate with *spreutaną (“to sprout”) from Proto-Indo-European *sper- (“to strew”). Compare North Frisian spraweli, Norwegian sprala, Swedish sprala.
examples: There were pillows on the floor, a few chairs, and four or five students sprawled here and there watching a football game.
A shrewd blow, it caught him off balance, and after one ineffectual stagger he sprawled backward and lay for a moment staring up in blank surprise
Bell sprawled full length to turn a Sandaza drive wide of the far post, but Saints had done enough to inflict Killie's first home defeat of the season.

senses: Any gathered or curled strip of fabric added as trim or decoration.
Disturbance; agitation; commotion.
ety: From Middle English ruffelen, perhaps from Old Norse hrufla (“to graze, scratch”) or Middle Low German ruffelen (“to wrinkle, curl”). Further origin unknown. Related to Middle Dutch ruyffelen, German Low German ruffeln. See English ruff.
examples: She loved the dress with the lace ruffle at the hem.
His dress was splendid; his hands glittered with rings, his snuff-box was covered with diamonds, and his ruffles were of the finest Mechlin lace.

senses: Of a dazzling lustre; glaring; bright; shining.
Resembling or characteristic of a glare, or angry look.
ety: From glare + -y.
examples: November 29, 1659, S. Hartlir, letter to Robert Boyle Bright, crystal glass is glary.
He gave me that glary look again, but he'd been overruled.

senses: A type of steam bath, popular in Russia (and in some parts of Alaska as well).
ety: From Russian ба́ня f (bánja). Doublet of bagnio, bain, and balaneion.
examples: The Russian public steam bath (banya) is a cultural hybrid which borrows freely from the Finnish sauna and the Turkish political detention centre.

senses: To know intuitively or by immediate perception.
ety: A back-formation from intuition and intuitive; compare Latin intuitus (“observed; considered”), perfect participle of intueor (“to look at, upon or towards; to observe, regard; to consider, contemplate”), from in- (“in, inside”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁én (“in”)) + tueor (“to look or gaze at”). Related to tuition, tutor.
examples: Bhandat frowned. The words had made no impression on him. And Mr Biswas knew for sure then, what he had intuited and dismissed: Bhandat was deaf.

senses: One of the landowning Dutch grandees of the Dutch colony of New Amsterdam, especially after it became a British possession renamed as New York.
ety: Borrowed from Dutch patroon (“patron saint; boss”), from Middle Dutch patroon, from Latin patrōnus (“protector; patron”). Doublet of padrone, patron, Patronus, and pattern.
examples: Dr. Tucker accompanied us on our return; and we made a call on General Van Rensselaer. He is the Patroon, or Lord of the Manor here; and is considered the greatest landholder in the United States.
In the United States the labourer is a freeman, lives on good substance, and being an honest man, neither fears nor envies the richest patroon about him.

senses: To take away by force; to carry away (a human being) wrongfully and usually with violence or deception; to kidnap.
ety: From Latin abductus, perfect passive participle of abduco (“to lead away”), from ab (“away”) + duco (“to lead”). * (physiology): Back-formation from abduction.
examples: That same night he had by force abducted the president and the secretary of the club, and had taken them, much against their will upon a voyage in the wonderful air-ship, the “Albatross,” which he had constructed.

senses: Synonym of daikon, particularly its Indian varieties.
ety: Borrowed from Hindi मूली (mūlī, “[Indian] radish”) (feminine of मूल (mūl)), from Sauraseni Prakrit 𑀫𑀽𑀮 (mūla), from Sanskrit मूल (mūla).
examples: Particularly delicious was mooli stuffed paratha—rich, flaky and filled with a fragrant grated radish mixture.
This is thanks to the introduction of a wider range of radish varieties into supermarkets, especially the long-rooted ‘mooli’ types from Japan.

senses: An authority on any subject.
ety: Borrowed from Iranian Persian آیَتُاللّٰه (âyato-l-lâh), from Classical Persian آیَةُاللّٰه (āyatu-l-lāh), from Arabic آيَةُ ٱللَّٰهِ (ʔāyatu llāhi, “sign of God”, from آيَة (ʔāya, “sign”) + اللّٰه (allāh, “God”)).
examples: P.S. This writer does NOT speak as the Ayatollah of SM. (There isn't one.) If you really want to know more, talk to sadomasochists, or at least do some reading if you're too scared to ask.

senses: Controlled or guided by a central authority, as in an economy.
ety: Borrowed from French dirigiste, from diriger (“to run, to direct”), from Latin dirigere (“to direct, to steer”).
examples: The repeated crises in dirigiste systems are in essence crises of information since the abolition of the market leaves the central planner bereft of that economic knowledge which is required for harmony.

Certainly, popular demands and the force of circumstances have already pushed the Biden administration towards a dirigiste programme of government-led recovery that has no real precedent since the 1960s.

senses: Lacking sense or meaning, often to the point of boredom or annoyance.
Purposeless; pointless.
ety: From Latin inānis (“empty, vain, useless”), of unknown origin.
examples: This supremely gifted kid told me that in the early elementary grades, the songs sung in music class were so inane that he wanted to skip grades already! Eventually he did, so better late than never.

God, if she had to listen to another conversation about some kid she didnʼt know—how Tina J. stole the stage at the talent show or Bobby R. won the tee ball game or any other number of inane accomplishments.

senses: An absorbent garment worn by a baby or toddler who does not yet have voluntary control of their bladder and bowels or by someone who is incontinent; a diaper.
ety: A diminutive in -y. The base is probably napkin but possibly French nappe directly (note that napkin is already a diminutive).
examples: You will notice that disposable nappies are sold in boy and girl versions. They vary in where the thickest padding is provided.

You could burn disposable nappies (not a very practical option); otherwise, it′s probably best to take a supply of large plastic bags or nappy sacks with you and to dispose of them as thoughtfully as you can.
In response we mailed hundreds of nappies to students in halls. On the nappy was a simple message, IT'S A LOT EASIER TO PUT ON A CONDOM.

senses: Capable of being cut; easily cut.
Having the appearance of being divided or broken.
ety: From Latin sectilis.
examples: Near-synonyms: sectionable, dissectable, dissectible, cuttable, sliceable
The beds, usually soft and sectile, and acted on with immense rapidity by river erosion, being converted into masses of striped jasper, often of great beauty and extreme hardness.

A good, though small, example of a sectile pavement will be found in the triforium of the cathedral of Aix-la-Chapelle, being no doubt a portion of that brought by Charles the Great from Rome or Ravenna.

senses: Of a person, given to vulgar verbal abuse; foul-mouthed.
Coarse, vulgar, or abusive.
Gross, vulgar.
Unscrupulous, evil.
ety: From Latin scurrīlis (“buffoon-like”) + -ous, from scurra (“a buffoon”).
examples: We have had our address used by scurrilous crooks in the past to gain assets by fraud.

senses: Having to do with acrobatic maneuvers, such as spins, twirls, and flips, performed by an airplane.
ety: Blend of aero- + acrobatic.
examples: Boobies are powerful, aerobatic fliers, and they can be challenging to photograph.

senses: Both global and local.
ety: Blend of global + local.
examples: Not so much wedded as welded to their airline seats, he and his amanuensis see the cities of the future as ‘glocal’ phenomena, where high-density urban centres are air-linked to intercontinental faubourgs.

senses: To bid more than (somebody else) in an auction.
ety: From out- + bid.
examples: Bengal outbidded those of Delhi; instead of searching for khalifahs for obtaining recognition, Sultan Sikandar Shah himself took the title .of Imam ul-Azam and Khalifat-ul-Muazzam.
You must understand that there are people who strive and save their whole lives to acquire something, and when they are simply outbidded or outfoxed by me, it is not taken with a delicate smile.

senses: A peccary (Tayassuidae spp.), especially a collared peccary (Dicotyles tajacu).
ety: From Spanish javalina, jabalina, feminine form of jabalí (“wild boar”), from Andalusian Arabic جَبَلِي (jabalī) (in خِنْزِير جَبَلِيّ (ḵinzīr jabaliyy, “mountain pig”)), from Arabic جَبَل (jabal, “mountain”). Cognate with Portuguese javalina, and similar in other Iberian languages.
examples: The Javelina (Peccari) is an animal peculiar so far as I know to Spanish America.
Some well-mounted heads of deer and one of an enormous black javeli projected from the walls.

senses: To reduce (an adult) to the state or status of an infant.
To treat (an adult) like a child.
ety: From infantile + -ize (“make into”).
examples: For too long, many of us have sought unity by binding ourselves together with the umbilical cords of dogma. They have done less and less to nurture us in recent years, and more and more to infantilize us.

senses: The contractile unit of the myofibril of a striated muscle.
ety: From sarco- (“flesh”) + -mere (“component”), from Ancient Greek σάρξ (sárx) and μέρος (méros).
examples: Specific proteins are responsible for the bands and zones within each sarcomere.
Of particular importance was the confirmation that the sarcomere lengths are instantaneously unstable for any reasonable assignment of parameters and number of sarcomeres, even as low as 100.

senses: A two-colour fabric pattern of broken checks.
Fabric with a houndstooth pattern; an item of clothing made with such fabric.
ety: From hound + -s- + tooth, from its appearance. Although the pattern itself is archaeologically found from time immemorial, the modern term is first attested in 1936.
examples: Sophisticated houndstooth checks highlight a toddler's jacket and hat.

senses: To prevent from happening.
To make of no use or value; to cancel out.
ety: From null + -ify.
examples: The persuasion that a thing is impossible, at once nullifies endeavour, and like the Turkish "it is fate," torporises activity and exertion.
It nullifies the night / from overkill

senses: A member of the order Alcyonacea, comprising the soft corals.
ety: From gorgon + -ian.
examples: Some gorgonians, living in shallow, sunlit waters, tend to be brightly coloured – gold, purple, red – and flex softly in the currents.

senses: Having frills; frilled.
Over-elaborate or showy in character or appearance.
ety: From frill + -y.
examples: Ms. Grant was dressed up as Little Bo Peep and had on a huge, frilly skirt that was held out with a hoop at the bottom.
The one she showed me has this frilly white skirt with blue bows on it.

senses: A simple computer speaker.
A pager (wireless telecommunication device).
A broadcast interview taking place over the telephone (originally having to include a beeping sound to indicate that it was not a live broadcast).
ety: From beep + -er.
examples: The Controls option enables you to resize and move a currently displayed window, as well as toggle the PC beeper.
No stages, front pages, no phones, no beepers
Radio "beepers" are easy: all you need is a telephone, and you can basically have an overseas conversation with any DJ or radio news director in America.

senses: Marked or grooved with ruts.
ety: From rut + -ed.
examples: It was as much as part of her days as stale bread and the blisters on her toes after a long day of walking the hard, rutted road.

senses: Damnedest; one's best effort.
ety: From darned + -est.
examples: I did my darnedest to stay awake.

senses: An instance of the interjection.
A pleasure coach.
ety: 1772, UK, probably alteration of French taïaut (interjection used in deer-hunting), from Middle French tahou, tayo, from Old French taho, ta ho, tielau (interjection given to hounds to return) (second half of 13th century), composed of ta (particle used to prod animals) + ho ! (“halt!, hold!”). More at ho.
examples: Alright, I'll give them the old tallyho.
They could not come to-day; there would have been hardly room for them in the tallyho.

senses: Any of a variety of coarse-grained crystalline metamorphic rocks with a foliated structure that allows easy division into slabs or slates.
ety: From French schiste, from Latin schistos lapis (“the stone that is easy to split”), from Ancient Greek σχιστός (skhistós, “splittable”), from σχίζω (skhízō, “to split”).
examples: Although it shows under the microscope traces of the original gabbro structure and of the original gabbro minerals, no one would hesitate from a microscopical examination to class it with the schists.
Millions of years ago the mica schists surrounding the old Brandberg West Mine became folded and concertinaed by enormous horizontal pressures.

senses: To display or express (emotions, mental states, etc.) openly, particularly while acting, and especially in an excessive manner.
To deliver (a speech), say (lines of a play, words), etc., in a dramatic or emotional manner, especially if overly so.
To display (excessive) emotion, especially while acting.
To express a virtual action, presented to other users as a graphic or reported speech, rather than sending a straightforward message.
To perform a short action, such as a gesture or a dance move, which may be seen by other players but does not have any effect on gameplay.
ety: The verb is a back-formation from emotion.
examples: In the Latin category, dancers begin the round in carnival mode, bouncing and curving voltas traveling down the length of the floor, emoting happy celebration in a Brazilianesque samba.
She doesn't smile much; she doesn't emote. Shannen is still.
Clint Eastwood, huh? You don't see him emoting all over the place, and what woman doesn't want to get down with "Dirty Harry," huh?

senses: A formal meeting, especially of a judicial or ecclesiastical body.
Those people present at such a meeting.
ety: From Latin sederunt (“there were sitting”).
examples: They held a sederunt, and were filled with tremulous joy, for, in spite of their familiarity with all the other worlds and cycles, they had a very human awe of things sent from Ghostland.

senses: The sound of something solid landing.
ety: Onomatopoeic. Compare plunk.
examples: I just heard a plonk – did something fall down in the kitchen?

senses: Rural, rustic; unsophisticated.
ety: From countrify + -ed.
examples: Although houses and factories appeared in great profusion in the 1930s, there still remain odd groups of cottages dating from an earlier and more countrified period.
There was this hot little countrified sistah who had caught my eye during the beginning of freshman year, but I just hadn't had a chance to work my way around to her yet.

senses: Powdered spice made from dried and ground fruits of sweet pepper (bell pepper) or chili pepper (cultivars of Capsicum annuum), or mixtures of these (used especially in Hungarian cooking).
A variety of the spice.
A bright reddish orange colour resembling that of the ground spice.
ety: Borrowed from Hungarian paprika, from Serbo-Croatian pàprika, from pȁpar, from Proto-Slavic *pьpьrь, from Latin piper, from Ancient Greek πέπερι (péperi, “pepper”), from Indo-Aryan; compare Sanskrit पिप्पलि (pippali, “long pepper”). Akin to paprikash.
examples: As a condiment in food, paprika is reputed to be strongly aphrodisiac.
California is taking the lead, producing a paprika that is more standardized and more uniformly available than the European growers offer.
Using the trio of paprikas gives more flavour than you'd get using a single paprika.
